quiz.q: In the restaurant analogy, which part plays the role of the API?
quiz.explain: The customer is the front-end, the kitchen is the back-end, and the waiter is the API mediating every order (request) and served dish (response).

quiz.q: Why is MuleSoft called a low-code tool?
options: It has no scripting language at all
Anypoint Studio generates XML code behind the drag-and-drop components
It runs code only on low-memory servers
quiz.explain: You mostly drag and drop; Studio writes the XML in the background, so very little code is written by hand.

quiz.q: Which statement about APIs and web services is correct according to the lecture?
options: All APIs are web services, but not all web services are APIs
APIs and web services are unrelated
All web services are APIs, but not all APIs are web services
quiz.explain: A web service is an API that communicates over a network/the internet; APIs such as library or OS APIs are not web services.

quiz.q: Why is a JSON message lighter than the same data in XML?
options: JSON is compressed automatically by HTTP
XML needs an opening and a closing tag for every value, adding extra text
quiz.explain: The tags make XML heavier for the same data, so REST with JSON uses fewer resources.

quiz.q: An API returns employees who resigned on a past date, and the same request arrives 20 times a day. What does the lecture recommend?
options: Move the data to an FTP server
Query the database every time to be safe
Cache the result the first time and serve repeat requests from cache
quiz.explain: The date is in the past, so the answer will never change — ideal for caching. Data that can change (e.g. 'resigned as of today') should not be cached.

quiz.q: Which design language is used for SOAP services?
quiz.explain: SOAP services are described with WSDL (Web Service Description Language); REST APIs are designed with RAML.

quiz.q: Which message format does SOAP accept?
options: JSON, XML, HTML and plain text
quiz.explain: SOAP accepts and returns only XML. REST is the one that accepts multiple formats.

quiz.q: What do MuleSoft developers typically do with SOAP services?
options: Convert all REST APIs to SOAP
Create new SOAP services for every project
quiz.explain: REST is created and consumed; SOAP is mostly consumed, since it lives in legacy systems.

quiz.q: In which environment do business users or clients test the application against business requirements and give sign-off?
quiz.explain: UAT = User Acceptance Testing by users. SIT/QA is the testing team; Pre-Prod is for performance testing.

quiz.q: Which environment is used for performance (load) testing to decide memory, CPU and number of servers?
quiz.explain: The slide says "Preprod – Performance Testing – QA team"; results decide how much memory/CPU the app needs.

quiz.q: A bank's primary data centre in Mumbai goes down. What keeps customers served?
options: A DR (Disaster Recovery) replica in a second data centre
quiz.explain: DR is a replica of production in another data centre that takes over if the primary fails. It is expensive, so it exists mainly in banks/financial institutions.

quiz.q: When and by whom are production deployments usually done?
options: Automatically whenever code is saved in Studio
By UAT users after sign-off, at any time
In non-business hours by a separate deployment team, after approvals
During business hours by the developer directly
quiz.explain: A separate production team deploys with permissions and approvals, typically at night; the developer guides and then checks the app.

cards.back: Application Programming Interface — a piece of code that lets two or more systems communicate and exchange data.
Most code is generated by the tool; in MuleSoft, Studio generates **XML** behind drag-and-drop.
Customer = front-end, waiter = **API**, kitchen = back-end; order = request, served food = response.
The same balance API serves net banking (web), Android and iOS — the API is language independent.
All web services are APIs, but not all APIs are web services. A web service is an API accessed over a network (instructor: over the internet).
REpresentational State Transfer — uses HTTP; accepts JSON, XML, HTML, plain text; lightweight, scalable, cacheable; designed with **RAML**.
Simple Object Access Protocol — XML only; HTTP/SMTP/UDP; more bandwidth; stricter; designed with **WSDL**; mostly legacy.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — the protocol REST uses to transfer requests and responses.
RAML designs REST APIs; WSDL describes SOAP services. Both define resources, request/response schemas, examples and security schemes.
When an existing system already exposes SOAP, or for a highly secure, strictly contracted enterprise service. New APIs use REST.
JSON is lighter (no opening/closing tags), easier to read and uses fewer resources.
In files on FTP/SFTP servers used by scheduled/batch integrations — not normal API bodies.
Temporary memory (part of server memory) that stores a previous result so repeat requests reuse it instead of redoing the work.
Only when the data does not change (or rarely changes), e.g. employees who resigned on a past date. Changing data would go stale.
Design → Develop → Secure → Deploy → Monitor.

cards.front: What is designed before building an API?
cards.back: Request, response with examples, data format, error response, security, and the resource path (e.g. `/db`).
Dev → SIT/QA → UAT → Pre-Prod (performance) → Prod, plus DR. Many companies use only 3–4.
System Integration Testing by the testing team — detailed testing of all scenarios and error responses, "like a critic".
User Acceptance Testing — business users or clients validate requirements and give **sign-off**.
Each has its own servers, database and connected systems (e.g. Salesforce) so dev, testing, validation and live traffic don't interfere.
A replica of production in a separate data centre that takes over if the primary fails. Expensive; mainly in banks.
Done in **non-business hours** by a separate deployment team with approvals; the developer guides and then observes.
An older system still in use — where SOAP services are mostly found.
